new_statements.quote: p. 338: "De toegevoegde lettergreep doet den klemtoon niet verspringen, zoodat, in de hier boven aangehaalde Lòda'sche woorden, de klemtoon steeds op de twee-na-laatste lettergreep valt." p. 356: "In het Lòd. krijgt men ook geen verandering in klemtoon, wanneer er aan een woord, overeenkomende met een zelfde uit een ander dialect een verlengstuk wordt toegevoegd, zooals wij boven gezien hebben: àké = ākéré; tébi = tébini; udo = ūdomo; ngiri = ngīriki, enz. Maar komen er aan de woorden in 't Lòd. achterzetsels of grammaticale achtervoegsels, dàn verspringt de klemtoon op de vòòrlaatste lettergreep van 't aldus verlengde woord."
new_statements.translation: p. 338: "The added syllable does not shift the stress, so that in the Lòda words cited above the stress always falls on the antepenultimate syllable." p. 356: "In Lòda one likewise gets no change of stress when a word corresponding to the same word in another dialect receives an extension, as we saw above: àké = ākéré; tébi = tébini; udo = ūdomo; ngiri = ngīriki, etc. But when postpositions or grammatical suffixes are attached to words in Lòda, then the stress jumps to the penultimate syllable of the word thus extended."
new_statements.citation: van Baarda, M. J. 1904. Het Lòda'sch in vergelijking met het Galela'sch dialect op Halmaheira, gevolgd door Lòda'sche teksten en verhalen. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde van Nederlandsch-Indië 56: 317-450
new_statements.locator: pp. 338 and 356 (Rosetta scan spreads 12 and 21; supporting remarks pp. 341, 357, 385)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (38 sideways spreads = BKI 56 pp. 316-391, no text layer), its scanned, and the page crops pages/p. 338), p. 356), p. 357), p. 341), p. 385). I also re-rendered spread 21 myself (page renders, rotated) and saved a crop of the whole p. 356 paragraph as pages/noted in, stamp) because the held 300-dpi crop starts one line into the quoted sentence. Quote check. p. 338 (the scanned text; crop, page header "338 HET LÒDA'SCH, IN VERGELIJKING MET HET"): "De toegevoegde lettergreep doet den klemtoon niet verspringen, zoodat, in de hier boven aangehaalde Lòda'sche woorden, de klemtoon steeds op de twee-na-laatste lettergreep valt." - verbatim, directly after the list "ngunu = ngūnungu:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Loda stress is placed as in Galela (penultimate) except that (a) the echo-vowel syllable Loda adds to many roots (ngunu > ngūnungu, tjala > tjālana) does not count, so such roots surface with antepenultimate stress in citation form, and (b) enclitic postpositions and grammatical suffixes are counted, so stress moves to the penult of the whole extended word (gòla > gòlā-ka; pònga-sa = wòngan'-īsa; tumu-ku = tumun'-ūku), unlike Galela where suffixes leave root stress alone. Reduplicants are clipped so that their stress is penultimate (p. 385).
new_statements.exceptions: Echo-vowel roots stressed on the antepenult in isolation (p. 338); a few cognates whose stress differs from Galela (p. 341: mogiōwo = Gal. mogìoko '10', pālungu = pangilū 'bullet'); the postposition òka loses its o after a-final and o-final words and the word's final syllable then takes the stress (p. 357: gòla: gòlāka; ādono: adonō-ka).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root plus enclitic postposition/suffix = one stress domain); framed throughout as Lòda-versus-Galela differences; citation forms of echo-vowel roots are antepenult. The description is of the Baru tribe's Lòda (van Baarda p. 321), i.e. Loloda lolo1264, not of the Laba/Kedi villages; van Baarda p. 321 says the four tribes' dialects differ only slightly. No statement about Laba speech itself exists in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: laba1241 (ISO lau; Ethnologue 'Laba', alt. Kedi, South Loloda; 2,000 speakers in 4 villages at the south end of Loloda district, NW Halmahera, incl. Laba Besar and Laba Kecil in Voorhoeve 1988's village list) is a Glottolog 5.3 Bookkeeping/spurious code: Glottolog merges it into Loloda lolo1264 on the strength of van Baarda 1904 and the surveys of Grimes & Grimes 1984 and Voorhoeve 1988. The two surveys, however, treat 'South Loloda' as Galela-like: Ethnologue says 'Phonology like Galela [gbi]' and Voorhoeve 1988 §2.4.2 says the southern variant 'although nominally Loloda is in fact a variant of Galela' (gale1259; Galela stress is penultimate per Shelden 1989). The quoted statement describes the Lòda of the Baru tribe (van Baarda 1904 p. 321) = lolo1264, the same statement already credited to lolo1264 in this reading; van Baarda p. 318-321 names Laba as one of the four Loda tribes whose dialects differ only slightly. A 2022 deixis paper from Desa Kedi (Sakalati) labels the local language 'bahasa Loloda' and its sample sentence shows Loloda j-forms rather than Galela d-forms. No source describes Laba speech itself.

new_statements.quote: In Galela the penultimate syllable usually carries the stress, and stress placement is not affected by suffixation. In Loda, although there are words which carry the stress on the penultimate syllable, the majority of them have the accent on the antepenultimate syllable. It is a peculiarity of this dialect that when suffixes are added to a word, the accent shifts towards the antepenultimate syllable of the affixed word. This causes the language to sound quite different <from Galela>.

new_statements.relation_note: The existing statement (van Baarda 1904, read as 'fixed: penultimate syllable') and Stokhof's note differ in two places. (a) Placement: Stokhof says the majority of Loda words have antepenultimate accent; the catalog's reading is penultimate. Stokhof's antepenult claim does match van Baarda 1904 p. 338 ('De toegevoegde lettergreep doet den klemtoon niet verspringen, zoodat.. de klemtoon steeds op de twee-na-laatste lettergreep valt'): the added echo syllable does not attract stress, so echo-extended words (a very large class) surface with antepenult stress. (b) Suffixation: Stokhof says the accent shifts to the ANTEPENULT of the affixed word, but van Baarda 1904 p. 356 says explicitly 'dàn…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Stokhof's editorial note (a paraphrase of the notes accompanying van Baarda's 1904 questionnaire), most Loda words carry the accent on the antepenultimate syllable, a minority on the penult; when suffixes are added the accent moves to the antepenultimate syllable of the suffixed word. The list forms themselves carry grave/acute/macron/breve marks that, under the Galela conventions of list 79 (p. 121), mark vowel quality/length, with stress marked only when non-penultimate; 1.2.2 adds 'Some diacritics are not clear', so stress cannot be read reliably off the entries.
new_statements.exceptions: 'there are words which carry the stress on the penultimate syllable' (a minority, per the note). The Galela article-like 'o' before nouns is absent in Loda.
new_statements.identity_note: Stokhof's list no. 80 is van Baarda's Loda, i.e. Loloda as spoken by the Baru tribe (van Baarda 1904 pp. 318-321), which Glottolog files as lolo1264; Laba (laba1241, Ethnologue's Kedi/South Loloda villages) is a Bookkeeping node and no source describes Laba speech itself. Van Baarda p. 321 says the four Loda tribes (Baru, Bakulu, Kedi, Laba) differ only slightly in dialect; Voorhoeve 1988 (read earlier) says the southern 'Loloda' is in fact a variant of Galela, which has plain penultimate stress.

readall_conflicts: Stokhof 1980 (p. 149) and van Baarda 1904 disagree on what suffixation does: Stokhof says the accent shifts to the antepenultimate syllable of the affixed word, van Baarda (p. 356, with examples gòla > gòläka, kurünga > kurungä-ka) says it jumps to the penultimate syllable of the extended word. Stokhof's note is an editorial paraphrase of the questionnaire notes, so the primary article wins on that point. The two sources agree that a large class of Loda words surfaces with antepenultimate stress (van Baarda p. 338: the added echo syllable never takes the stress), which is why Stokhof calls antepenult the majority pattern; the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate' reading is a stem-level abstraction (penult of the base as in Galela, echo syllable not counted, suffixes counted). A surface-syllable count over the vocabulary would instead give antepenult-majority, so the catalog entry should carry that caveat.
